title: Amsterdam court orders Uber to reinstate drivers 'robo-fired' by automated fraud detection
description: The District Court of Amsterdam issued a default judgment on 14 April 2021 ordering Uber to reinstate six drivers — five in the UK, one in the Netherlands — dismissed after Uber's automated systems flagged them for alleged fraudulent activity, ruling this qualified as a decision based solely on automated processing prohibited under GDPR Article 22(1) absent an applicable exemption. The drivers were represented by the App Drivers & Couriers Union and Worker Info Exchange. In a contested appeal on 4 April 2023, the Amsterdam Court of Appeal again ruled largely against Uber (and against Ola Cabs in a related case), rejecting the companies' claim that human reviewers had meaningfully checked the algorithmic decisions, describing such review as 'not much more than a purely symbolic act.'

history.note: Initial Edition 1.1 content. A reported ~€100,474 damages figure for the April 2021 ruling could not be independently verified against a primary source and is omitted from this record.

root_cause: Uber's fraud-detection system flagged and deactivated drivers' accounts based on automated risk-scoring, with human 'review' that courts found to be superficial rather than a genuine check on the algorithm's output, violating GDPR's restriction on solely automated decisions with significant effects on individuals.

relationships.reason: A guaranteed, genuine human-review right before an algorithm deactivates a worker's account directly addresses this ruling's finding.
This is the first ruling to enforce GDPR Article 22 protections against automated platform-worker terminations.
